about: Separation Processes 1 (CENG40009) is a 5-credit core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, taught in the Spring term. No official Imperial module descriptor was found. An undated third-party UC Education Abroad Program (UCEAP) course listing describes it as covering the principles of diffusional separations and the mathematical and graphical methods used to analyse and design them, applying them to distillation, absorption and liquid–liquid extraction in both staged and continuous-contact equipment. A later UCEAP listing (last reviewed 2024-25) adds absorption and stripping of single solutes, extraction between immiscible phases and brief consideration of economic viability. The breakdown into topics and their order are this pack's own, built from these descriptions. No module-level assessment breakdown was found on official pages.

notes.body:
Diffusional separations
Distillation, absorption, stripping and liquid–liquid extraction all work the same way: two phases are brought into contact, a component transfers between them because it is not at equilibrium, and the phases are then separated. The phase-equilibrium relation sets the limit of what one contact can achieve, and mass transfer rates set how close real equipment gets to that limit.

The equilibrium (ideal or theoretical) stage
An equilibrium stage is a contact in which the leaving streams are in equilibrium with each other. Real trays fall short of this, which is handled with stage efficiencies. Counting equilibrium stages is the central design calculation of this module.

Vapour–liquid equilibrium (VLE)
For an ideal liquid mixture and an ideal gas, Raoult's law gives each partial pressure:
p_i = x_i P_i*(T), so y_i = x_i P_i*/P
where P_i* is the pure-component vapour pressure (from Antoine's equation or tables). The K-value K_i = y_i/x_i = P_i*/P.

Relative volatility
α_AB = K_A/K_B = (y_A/x_A)/(y_B/x_B). For an ideal system α = P_A*/P_B*, which changes only slowly with temperature, so a constant average α is often used. For a binary mixture:
y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x]
The larger α is, the easier the separation; α = 1 means no separation by simple distillation (as at an azeotrope).

Worked example: benzene–toluene at 100 °C
Approximate vapour pressures at 100 °C: benzene 180 kPa, toluene 74 kPa, so α ≈ 2.4.
- Bubble-point liquid at P = 101.3 kPa and 100 °C: x_B P_B* + (1 − x_B)P_T* = P, so x_B = (101.3 − 74)/(180 − 74) = 0.258.
- The vapour in equilibrium: y_B = 180 × 0.258/101.3 = 0.458.
The vapour is richer in the more volatile component, which is the basis of distillation.

Bubble and dew points
- Bubble point: temperature (at fixed P) at which a liquid first starts to boil; Σ K_i x_i = 1.
- Dew point: temperature at which a vapour first starts to condense; Σ y_i/K_i = 1.
- Between them, a mixture is two-phase. A T–x–y diagram shows both curves; an x–y diagram plots the equilibrium curve against the 45° line.

Gas–liquid equilibrium: Henry's law
For a sparingly soluble gas in a liquid, p_A = H x_A, or y = m x with m = H/P. Large m means low solubility. Henry's constants rise with temperature for most gases, so gases are less soluble in hot liquids.

Non-ideal systems
Strongly non-ideal liquids need activity coefficients (modified Raoult's law, p_i = γ_i x_i P_i*). Azeotropes, where y = x, cannot be crossed by ordinary distillation.

Exam tips: check which component is the more volatile, quote α with the temperature range, and sketch the x–y curve to sense-check every answer.

What a flash does
A flash (equilibrium flash or flash vaporisation) is a single equilibrium stage. A liquid feed is heated and/or let down in pressure into a drum, part of it vaporises, and the vapour and liquid leave in equilibrium. It gives only a modest separation but is used everywhere: as a first rough cut, after reactors and in refinery and gas processing units.

Balances for a flash
Feed F with composition z_i; vapour V with y_i; liquid L with x_i.
- Total: F = V + L.
- Component: F z_i = V y_i + L x_i.
- Equilibrium: y_i = K_i x_i.
Let ψ = V/F (the vaporised fraction).

Binary flash: lever rule
For a binary at fixed T and P, the two-phase compositions are fixed by equilibrium alone. With constant K values:
x_A = (1 − K_B)/(K_A − K_B), y_A = K_A x_A.
The vapour fraction then follows from the lever rule:
ψ = V/F = (z − x)/(y − x).

Worked example
A 50 mol% benzene–toluene feed is flashed at conditions where K_benzene = 1.6 and K_toluene = 0.65.
- x = (1 − 0.65)/(1.6 − 0.65) = 0.368; y = 1.6 × 0.368 = 0.589.
- ψ = (0.5 − 0.368)/(0.589 − 0.368) = 0.595, so about 60% of the feed vaporises.
- Check: 0.595 × 0.589 + 0.405 × 0.368 = 0.500.

Graphical method
On the x–y diagram, the component balance rearranges to an operating line through the point (z, z) on the 45° line:
y = −[(1 − ψ)/ψ] x + z/ψ
The flash compositions are where this line meets the equilibrium curve. A slope of −(L/V) means the more vapour you make, the shallower the line.

Multicomponent flash: Rachford–Rice
For several components at given T and P, substituting x_i = z_i/[1 + ψ(K_i − 1)] into Σy_i − Σx_i = 0 gives
Σ z_i(K_i − 1)/[1 + ψ(K_i − 1)] = 0,
which is solved for ψ by iteration (Newton's method is common). A physical answer needs 0 < ψ < 1; at the bubble point ψ = 0, at the dew point ψ = 1.

Adiabatic flash
If the drum is adiabatic, an energy balance (F h_F = V H_V + L h_L) is added and the drum temperature becomes an unknown, so T and ψ are found together.

Why one stage is not enough
A single flash cannot produce two pure products, because the vapour and liquid are only one equilibrium step apart. Stacking stages with counter-current flow (a distillation column) overcomes this.

Exam tips: check the feed lies between the bubble and dew points (0 < ψ < 1), use the lever rule for binaries, and confirm with a component balance.

notes.h: Binary distillation: column balances and McCabe–Thiele
notes.body:
The continuous column
A distillation column stacks many stages in counter-current flow: vapour rises from a reboiler at the bottom, liquid flows down from a condenser at the top, and the feed enters part-way. The section above the feed is the rectifying (enriching) section; below it is the stripping section. Reflux L returned from the condenser and boil-up V′ from the reboiler create the two counter-current streams.

Overall balances
F = D + B and Fz = Dx_D + Bx_B, so D = F(z − x_B)/(x_D − x_B).
Example: F = 100 kmol/h, z = 0.40, x_D = 0.95, x_B = 0.05 gives D = 38.9 and B = 61.1 kmol/h.

Constant molal overflow (CMO)
If the components have similar molar latent heats and heat effects are small, each mole of vapour that condenses on a stage vaporises about one mole of liquid. Then L and V are constant within each section, and the operating lines are straight. This is the key assumption of the McCabe–Thiele method.

Operating lines
- Rectifying section, from a balance round the top: y = [R/(R + 1)]x + x_D/(R + 1), where R = L/D is the reflux ratio. It passes through (x_D, x_D).
- Stripping section: y = (L′/V′)x − Bx_B/V′. It passes through (x_B, x_B).
For the example with R = 2: L = 77.8, V = 116.7 kmol/h; rectifying line y = 0.667x + 0.317.

Feed condition and the q-line
q = heat needed to turn 1 mol of feed into saturated vapour ÷ molar latent heat; for partly vaporised feed it equals the liquid fraction.
- Saturated liquid: q = 1. Saturated vapour: q = 0. Subcooled liquid: q > 1. Superheated vapour: q < 0.
- Section flows: L′ = L + qF and V = V′ + (1 − q)F.
- The q-line, y = [q/(q − 1)]x − z/(q − 1), passes through (z, z); the two operating lines meet on it. For a saturated liquid feed it is vertical at x = z.
For the example (q = 1): L′ = 177.8, V′ = 116.7, so the stripping line is y = 1.524x − 0.0262. Both lines meet at (0.40, 0.583).

Stepping off stages
Start at (x_D, x_D) for a total condenser. Move horizontally to the equilibrium curve (a stage: y leaving, x leaving in equilibrium), then vertically to the operating line (the balance linking passing streams). Repeat, switching from the rectifying to the stripping line once a step crosses the intersection; that step is the optimal feed stage. A partial reboiler counts as one equilibrium stage.
For the example with α = 2.5, R = 2, stepping gives 13 theoretical stages including the reboiler, with the feed on stage 7 from the top.

Partial condenser
A partial condenser returns liquid reflux and takes vapour product, and acts as an extra equilibrium stage.

Exam tips: label every line on your sketch, show the q-line, and state whether your stage count includes the reboiler.

notes.h: Reflux ratio, limiting cases and stage efficiency
notes.body:
Choosing the reflux ratio is the main design trade-off in distillation. More reflux moves the operating lines away from the equilibrium curve, so fewer stages are needed, but more vapour must be generated, so energy costs and column diameter rise.

Total reflux and the Fenske equation
At total reflux no product is withdrawn (R → ∞), the operating lines coincide with the 45° line and the number of stages is the minimum, N_min. For constant α:
N_min = ln[(x_D/(1 − x_D)) × ((1 − x_B)/x_B)] / ln α
N_min counts all equilibrium stages, including a partial reboiler.
Example: x_D = 0.95, x_B = 0.05, α = 2.5: N_min = ln(19 × 19)/ln 2.5 = 5.889/0.916 = 6.4 stages.

Minimum reflux
As R falls, the operating lines approach the equilibrium curve. At R_min they touch it (a pinch) and an infinite number of stages is needed. For ideal systems the pinch is usually at the intersection of the q-line and the equilibrium curve, (x′, y′):
R_min/(R_min + 1) = (x_D − y′)/(x_D − x′)
Example: saturated liquid feed z = 0.40, α = 2.5: y′ = 2.5 × 0.4/(1 + 1.5 × 0.4) = 0.625. Then R_min/(R_min + 1) = (0.95 − 0.625)/(0.95 − 0.40) = 0.591, so R_min = 1.44.
For strongly non-ideal equilibrium curves the pinch can be tangential elsewhere, so always check the sketch.

Optimum reflux
Total cost (annualised capital plus operating) has a minimum at a modest multiple of R_min; a common rule of thumb is roughly 1.2–1.5 R_min (approximate heuristic). Our example with R = 2 is 1.38 R_min and needs 13 theoretical stages, about twice N_min. Shortcut correlations (such as Gilliland's) link N, N_min, R and R_min for quick estimates.

Stage efficiency
Real trays do not reach equilibrium.
- Overall efficiency E_o = number of theoretical stages ÷ number of actual trays. Example: 12 theoretical trays plus a reboiler with E_o = 0.7 needs 12/0.7 = 17.1, so 18 actual trays (always round up).
- Murphree vapour efficiency for tray n: E_MV = (y_n − y_n+1)/(y_n* − y_n+1), the actual change in vapour composition over the change if the vapour left in equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray. Example: y_n+1 = 0.50, y_n = 0.60, y_n* = 0.65 gives E_MV = 0.67.
- On a McCabe–Thiele diagram, Murphree efficiencies are used by drawing a pseudo-equilibrium curve that lies a fraction E_MV of the vertical distance from the operating line to the true equilibrium curve.

Effect of changing conditions (qualitative)
- Higher R: fewer stages, larger reboiler and condenser duties, larger diameter.
- Colder (subcooled) feed: q > 1, more boil-up needed but fewer stripping stages.
- Lower α (harder separation): both N_min and R_min rise sharply.

Exam tips: compute N_min and R_min first; they bracket the design and show whether your stage count is sensible.

notes.h: Gas absorption and stripping in staged columns
notes.body:
Absorption and stripping
- Absorption: a solute is removed from a gas by contacting it with a liquid solvent in which it dissolves (CO₂ into amine solutions, NH₃ into water, solvent vapours into oil).
- Stripping (desorption): the reverse, removing a dissolved solute from a liquid into a gas or steam.
They are usually operated as counter-current columns: gas enters at the bottom, liquid at the top.

Equilibrium and balances for dilute systems
For dilute solutes, Henry's law gives a straight equilibrium line y = m x, and total gas and liquid flows G and L are roughly constant. (For concentrated systems, work in solute-free mole ratios Y = y/(1 − y) and X = x/(1 − x) with carrier flows, which keeps the balance exact.)
Solute balance over the column: G(y_in − y_out) = L(x_out − x_in). The operating line has slope L/G and, for absorption, lies above the equilibrium line on an x–y diagram.

Minimum liquid rate
With less and less solvent, the outlet liquid approaches equilibrium with the entering gas: x_out → x_out* = y_in/m. Then
(L/G)_min = (y_in − y_out)/(x_out* − x_in)
and an infinite number of stages would be needed. Designs typically use L/G of about 1.2–2 times the minimum (approximate heuristic).

Worked example
Gas with y_in = 0.02, 90% recovery (y_out = 0.002), solute-free solvent (x_in = 0), equilibrium y = 1.5x.
- x_out* = 0.02/1.5 = 0.0133; (L/G)_min = 0.018/0.0133 = 1.35. (With x_in = 0 this equals m × fractional recovery.)
- Use 1.5 × minimum: L/G = 2.025; x_out = 0.018/2.025 = 0.0089.

Absorption factor and the Kremser equation
A = L/(mG), the ratio of the operating-line slope to the equilibrium-line slope.
- A > 1: the solvent can carry away more solute than the gas brings, so very high recoveries are possible with enough stages.
- A < 1: recovery is limited even with infinitely many stages.
For straight operating and equilibrium lines, the number of equilibrium stages for absorption is
N = ln{[(y_in − m x_in)/(y_out − m x_in)](1 − 1/A) + 1/A} / ln A
For the example, A = 2.025/1.5 = 1.35:
N = ln[10 × (1 − 0.741) + 0.741]/ln 1.35 = ln 3.333/0.300 = 4.0 stages.
For stripping the same form applies with the stripping factor S = mG/L = 1/A, written in liquid compositions.

Operating variables
- Absorption is favoured by low temperature (smaller m) and high pressure (m = H/P falls as P rises).
- Stripping is favoured by high temperature and low pressure, or by using steam.
- Chemical solvents (such as amines for CO₂) react with the solute, greatly increasing capacity, and are regenerated by stripping.

Graphical method
The McCabe–Thiele construction works for absorbers: draw equilibrium and operating lines and step between them from one end of the column to the other.

Exam tips: define A before using Kremser, check A > 1 for high recovery, and use mole ratios if the solute is not dilute.

notes.h: Continuous-contact (packed) columns: film theory, HTU and NTU
notes.body:
In a packed column, gas and liquid are in continuous contact over the wetted surface of the packing rather than in discrete stages. The design question becomes "how tall?", answered with transfer units.

Two-film theory
At the gas–liquid interface, each phase has a thin stagnant film where all the resistance to mass transfer is assumed to lie, and the interface itself is at equilibrium.
- Gas film: N_A = k_y(y − y_i). Liquid film: N_A = k_x(x_i − x).
- Interface compositions are hard to measure, so overall coefficients based on bulk compositions are used: N_A = K_y(y − y*), where y* = m x is the gas composition in equilibrium with the bulk liquid.
- For a straight equilibrium line: 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x. The two terms are the gas-film and liquid-film resistances.

Controlling resistance
- Highly soluble gases (small m, e.g. NH₃ in water): m/k_x is small, so the gas film controls.
- Sparingly soluble gases (large m, e.g. O₂ or CO₂ in water): the liquid film controls, and it is better to use the liquid-side overall coefficient K_x.
Example: k_y = 0.05, k_x = 0.5 kmol/m² s, m = 2: 1/K_y = 20 + 4 = 24, so K_y = 0.0417 kmol/m² s, with the gas film providing 20/24 = 83% of the resistance.

Height from a differential balance
For a dilute system, over a slice dZ of a column with cross-section area S and interfacial area a per unit packed volume:
G dy = K_y a (y − y*) dZ, where G is the gas molar flux (kmol/m² s).
Integrating gives Z = H_OG × N_OG with
- H_OG = G/(K_y a): height of an overall gas-phase transfer unit (m), reflecting how good the packing and flow conditions are.
- N_OG = ∫ dy/(y − y*) from y_out to y_in: number of overall gas-phase transfer units, reflecting how difficult the separation is.

Evaluating N_OG
- Straight operating and equilibrium lines: N_OG = (y_in − y_out)/Δy_lm, where Δy_lm is the log mean of (y − y*) at the two ends.
- Equivalent closed form: N_OG = [1/(1 − 1/A)] ln{(1 − 1/A)[(y_in − m x_in)/(y_out − m x_in)] + 1/A}.
- Very large A (equilibrium back-pressure negligible): N_OG = ln(y_in/y_out).
- Curved lines: integrate numerically.

Worked example (same duty as the staged absorber: y_in = 0.02, y_out = 0.002, x_in = 0, m = 1.5, L/G = 2.025)
- Ends: bottom y − y* = 0.02 − 1.5 × 0.0089 = 0.00667; top 0.002 − 0 = 0.002.
- Δy_lm = (0.00667 − 0.002)/ln(0.00667/0.002) = 0.00388.
- N_OG = 0.018/0.00388 = 4.64. With H_OG = 0.5 m, Z = 2.3 m.

Transfer units vs stages
N_OG and N differ unless A = 1. Height equivalent to a theoretical plate: HETP = H_OG × ln(1/A)/(1/A − 1). For A = 1.35, HETP = 0.5 × 1.157 = 0.58 m, consistent with 4.0 stages × 0.58 m ≈ 2.3 m.

Exam tips: state the two-film assumptions, identify the controlling film from m, and check N_OG with both the log-mean and closed-form expressions.

Principle
Liquid–liquid extraction separates a solute from a liquid feed (the carrier or diluent) by contacting it with a second, immiscible or partly miscible solvent in which the solute is more soluble. The solute-rich solvent phase is the extract; the depleted feed phase is the raffinate. Extraction is chosen when distillation is difficult or damaging: close-boiling mixtures, azeotropes, heat-sensitive products (pharmaceuticals, foods) or dilute solutes in water.

Distribution coefficient
At equilibrium, K_D = (solute concentration in extract)/(solute concentration in raffinate). Concentrations can be mass fractions or, more conveniently for immiscible systems, mass ratios (kg solute per kg solvent or carrier). Solvent choice balances a high K_D and selectivity, low mutual solubility, a density difference for easy settling, ease of recovery, safety and cost.

Immiscible solvents, constant K_D
Let F be the carrier mass, S the solvent mass, and define the extraction factor E = K_D S/F (solute carried by solvent ÷ solute left in carrier at equilibrium).
- Single stage: fraction of solute left in raffinate = 1/(1 + E).
- Crosscurrent (fresh solvent split equally over N stages, each with factor E/N): fraction left = 1/(1 + E/N)^N.
- Counter-current, N stages, all solvent fed at the opposite end: fraction left = (E − 1)/(E^(N+1) − 1) for E ≠ 1.

Worked example
K_D = 4 (mass-ratio basis), 100 kg carrier, 50 kg solvent in total, so E = 2.
- One stage: 1/3 = 33.3% left.
- Two crosscurrent stages with 25 kg each (E = 1 per stage): (1/2)² = 25% left.
- Two counter-current stages with 50 kg: (2 − 1)/(2³ − 1) = 1/7 = 14.3% left.
Counter-current operation makes the best use of a given amount of solvent, which is why extraction columns and mixer–settler cascades are run counter-currently.

Partially miscible systems: triangular diagrams
When the solvent and carrier dissolve in each other, compositions of the three-component system are plotted on an equilateral or right-angled triangle.
- The binodal (solubility) curve encloses the two-phase region.
- Tie lines join extract and raffinate compositions in equilibrium; they meet at the plait point, where the two phases become identical.
- The mixture point M lies on the straight line joining feed F and solvent S, positioned by the lever rule (FM/MS = S/F); the tie line through M gives the extract and raffinate.
- For counter-current cascades, a difference (operating) point is used to step off stages graphically.

Equipment
Mixer–settlers (one stage each, flexible, large hold-up), agitated columns and pulsed or packed columns (continuous counter-current contact), and centrifugal extractors (short contact time, for small density differences).

Exam tips: write the extraction factor clearly, compare crosscurrent and counter-current on the same total solvent, and on triangular diagrams always locate M with the lever rule before drawing tie lines.

notes.h: Mass transfer equipment: trays, packing and column sizing
notes.body:
The equilibrium-stage and transfer-unit calculations give the number of stages or the packed height. The equipment must then provide good contact between the phases and allow the vapour and liquid to flow without operating problems.

Tray (plate) columns
Liquid flows across each tray and down a downcomer to the tray below; vapour rises through openings in the tray and bubbles through the liquid.
- Sieve trays: simple perforated plates; cheap, but a narrower operating range.
- Valve trays: movable caps over holes that open with vapour rate, giving a wider operating range.
- Bubble-cap trays: older design that holds liquid at very low vapour rates; expensive.
Typical tray spacing is around 0.45–0.6 m (approximate).

Operating limits of trays
- Flooding: at high vapour or liquid rates, liquid backs up in the downcomers or is carried up by the vapour until the column fills; this sets the maximum capacity.
- Entrainment: at high vapour velocity, liquid droplets are carried to the tray above, lowering efficiency.
- Weeping (and dumping): at low vapour rates, liquid drains through the holes instead of flowing across the tray.
- The stable operating window lies between these limits.

Packed columns
- Random packings (rings and saddles such as Raschig and Pall rings) or structured packings (corrugated sheets) provide a large wetted surface.
- Performance is quoted as HETP or H_OG.
- Packing often suits small-diameter columns, corrosive systems (ceramic or plastic packings), low pressure-drop or vacuum duties, and foaming systems. Trays often suit large diameters, high liquid rates, dirty or fouling services and where side draws or cooling between stages are needed. (These are general heuristics.)
- Packed columns need good liquid distributors and redistributors to avoid channelling, and they too flood at high flow rates.

Column diameter from flooding
The vapour velocity at flooding is often estimated with a Souders–Brown form:
u_f = C √[(ρ_L − ρ_V)/ρ_V]
where C (m/s) comes from correlations that depend on tray spacing, liquid–vapour flow ratio and surface tension. Columns are designed at a fraction of flooding, often about 70–85% (approximate heuristic).

Worked example
C = 0.08 m/s, ρ_L = 800 kg/m³, ρ_V = 3 kg/m³, vapour flow 2 m³/s, design at 80% of flooding.
- u_f = 0.08 × √(797/3) = 1.30 m/s; design u = 1.04 m/s.
- Net area = 2/1.04 = 1.92 m², so D = √(4 × 1.92/π) = 1.56 m (before allowing for downcomer area, which makes the real column larger).

Column height
Height ≈ number of actual trays × tray spacing (or packed height), plus space at the top for disengagement and at the bottom for the liquid sump and reboiler return.

Energy
Distillation is energy-intensive: the reboiler duty is roughly the boil-up rate times the molar latent heat. Heat integration, lower reflux and alternative separations reduce energy use.

Exam tips: name the limiting phenomenon (flooding, entrainment or weeping) for each operating extreme, and show how diameter follows from vapour flow and allowable velocity.

α_AB = (y_A/x_A)/(y_B/x_B) = K_A/K_B; for ideal systems α = P_A*/P_B*.

Σ y_i/K_i = 1 (first drop of liquid forms).

Binary flash compositions with constant K

cards.f: Flash operating line on x–y diagram
cards.b: Passes through (z, z) with slope −L/V = −(1 − ψ)/ψ.

cards.f: ψ at bubble and dew points
cards.b: ψ = 0 at the bubble point, ψ = 1 at the dew point.
No heat added in the drum: an energy balance fixes the outlet temperature together with ψ.
Assumes equal molar latent heats and negligible heat effects, so L and V are constant in each section and operating lines are straight.
y = [R/(R + 1)]x + x_D/(R + 1); passes through (x_D, x_D).
y = (L′/V′)x − Bx_B/V′; passes through (x_B, x_B).

cards.f: q for a saturated liquid feed
cards.b: q = 1 (q-line vertical at x = z). Saturated vapour: q = 0 (horizontal).
L′ = L + qF and V = V′ + (1 − q)F.
y = [q/(q − 1)]x − z/(q − 1); passes through (z, z).
The step that crosses the intersection of the operating lines; switch lines there.
Acts as one equilibrium stage, so it is counted in the theoretical stage total.
No products withdrawn; operating lines on the 45° line; gives the minimum number of stages.
N_min = ln[(x_D/(1 − x_D))((1 − x_B)/x_B)]/ln α (constant α; includes the reboiler).
Reflux at which an operating line touches the equilibrium curve (a pinch), so infinitely many stages are needed.

cards.f: R_min for a pinch at the q-line intersection (x′, y′)
cards.b: R_min/(R_min + 1) = (x_D − y′)/(x_D − x′).
Roughly 1.2–1.5 × R_min (approximate heuristic; depends on energy and capital costs).
E_o = theoretical stages ÷ actual trays; round the actual number up.
E_MV = (y_n − y_n+1)/(y_n* − y_n+1), where y_n* is in equilibrium with the liquid leaving tray n.
Fewer stages (lower capital for height) but higher reboiler/condenser duty and larger column diameter.
Absorption transfers a solute from gas into a liquid solvent; stripping transfers it from a liquid into a gas or steam.
(L/G)_min = (y_in − y_out)/(x_out* − x_in) with x_out* = y_in/m (outlet liquid in equilibrium with inlet gas).
A = L/(mG): ratio of operating-line slope to equilibrium-line slope. A > 1 is needed for high recovery.
N = ln{[(y_in − m x_in)/(y_out − m x_in)](1 − 1/A) + 1/A}/ln A for straight lines.
Low temperature and high pressure (smaller m = H/P, higher solubility).

cards.f: Why use mole ratios for concentrated absorption?
cards.b: Carrier gas and solvent flows stay constant, so balances in Y = y/(1 − y) and X = x/(1 − x) are exact straight lines.
S = mG/L = 1/A; stripping needs S > 1 for high removal.
All mass transfer resistance lies in thin stagnant films on each side of the interface, which is at equilibrium.
1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x for a straight equilibrium line y = mx.
When m is small (highly soluble gas, e.g. NH₃ in water), so m/k_x ≪ 1/k_y.
Z = H_OG × N_OG.
G/(K_y a): height of one overall gas-phase transfer unit; depends on packing and flows.
∫dy/(y − y*); for straight lines = (y_in − y_out)/Δy_lm.

cards.f: N_OG when A is very large
cards.b: N_OG ≈ ln(y_in/y_out), since y* ≈ 0 throughout.
Height equivalent to a theoretical plate = H_OG ln(1/A)/(1/A − 1); equals H_OG when A = 1.
Extract: solvent-rich phase carrying the solute. Raffinate: the feed (carrier) phase after solute removal.
Solute concentration in extract ÷ solute concentration in raffinate at equilibrium.
E = K_D S/F (immiscible solvents, mass-ratio basis).
(E − 1)/(E^(N+1) − 1) for E ≠ 1, with fresh solvent.
Point on the binodal curve where tie lines shrink to zero length and the two liquid phases become identical.

cards.f: Mixture point M on a triangular diagram
cards.b: Lies on the line FS, with FM/MS = S/F (lever rule).

cards.f: When is extraction preferred to distillation?
cards.b: Close-boiling or azeotropic mixtures, heat-sensitive solutes, or dilute solutes where distillation would have to boil off most of the carrier (often water).
Excess vapour and/or liquid flow causes liquid to accumulate (downcomer backup or entrainment) until the column fills; sets maximum capacity.
At low vapour rates, liquid drains through tray holes instead of crossing the tray.
Liquid droplets carried up by high-velocity vapour to the tray above, reducing efficiency.
u_f = C √[(ρ_L − ρ_V)/ρ_V]; design at a fraction (often about 70–85%) of u_f.
Sieve: simple perforated plate, cheap, narrower turndown. Valve: movable caps give a wider operating range.
Small diameters, corrosive or foaming systems, low pressure drop or vacuum service.

cards.f: What HETP measures for a packing
cards.b: Height equivalent to a theoretical plate: packed height giving the same separation as one equilibrium stage.

questions.q: A binary mixture has constant relative volatility α = 2.5. What is the equilibrium vapour mole fraction of the more volatile component above a liquid with x = 0.4?
questions.why: y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x] = 1.0/(1 + 1.5 × 0.4) = 1.0/1.6 = 0.625. 1.0 is just αx with the denominator left out, which is impossible as a mole fraction unless the vapour is pure. 0.4 assumes the vapour has the liquid composition, which only holds when α = 1. 0.5 uses 1 + αx as the denominator instead of 1 + (α − 1)x.

questions.q: For a gas dissolving in water according to y = m x, what does a large value of m indicate?
options: The liquid is close to its bubble point
questions.why: For a given gas-phase mole fraction, the equilibrium liquid mole fraction is x = y/m, so a large m means little gas dissolves. A highly soluble gas has a small m. The value of m says nothing about the liquid's bubble point. Henry's law is usually applied with an ideal gas phase; m reflects solubility, not gas non-ideality.

questions.q: At 100 °C the vapour pressures of benzene and toluene are approximately 180 kPa and 74 kPa. Assuming Raoult's law, find (a) the relative volatility, and (b) the liquid composition that boils at 100 °C under 101.3 kPa and the composition of the vapour formed.
markScheme: Bubble-point equation x_B P_B* + (1 − x_B)P_T* = P (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For ideal mixtures α = P_B*/P_T* = 180/74 = 2.43. (b) At the bubble point the partial pressures add to the total pressure: x_B(180) + (1 − x_B)(74) = 101.3, so x_B = 27.3/106 = 0.258. The first vapour has y_B = 0.258 × 180/101.3 = 0.458 (toluene 0.542). Check with α: 2.43 × 0.258/(1 + 1.43 × 0.258) = 0.458.

questions.q: A binary feed with z = 0.50 is flashed, giving a liquid with x = 0.40 and a vapour with y = 0.65. What fraction of the feed is vaporised?
questions.why: V/F = (z − x)/(y − x) = 0.10/0.25 = 0.40. 0.60 is (y − z)/(y − x), the liquid fraction L/F. 1.5 is (y − z)/(z − x), the ratio L/V. 0.67 is (z − x)/(y − z), the ratio V/L.

questions.q: In the Rachford–Rice method for a multicomponent flash, a solution with ψ = V/F greater than 1 indicates that
options: the feed is above its dew point at the flash conditions, so it is all vapour
the feed is below its bubble point, so it is all liquid
more vapour leaves than feed enters, so the balance is wrong
the K-values must all be less than 1
questions.why: If the iteration gives ψ > 1, there is no two-phase region at that T and P: the feed is superheated vapour. A subcooled liquid feed would give ψ < 0. It does not mean the balance is broken; it signals that the assumed two-phase state is impossible. If all K-values were less than 1, the mixture would be below its bubble point, which leads to ψ < 0, not ψ > 1.

questions.q: A 50 mol% benzene–toluene mixture is flashed at a temperature and pressure where K_benzene = 1.6 and K_toluene = 0.65. Find the liquid and vapour compositions and the fraction vaporised, and check your answer with the Rachford–Rice equation.
A column operates with reflux ratio R = 3. What is the slope of the rectifying-section operating line?
questions.why: The slope is L/V = R/(R + 1) = 3/4 = 0.75. 3 is R itself, which is L/D rather than L/V. 0.25 is 1/(R + 1), the factor that multiplies x_D in the intercept. 1.33 is (R + 1)/R, the inverse of the slope, which would be greater than 1, impossible for the rectifying line.

questions.q: How does the q-line appear on an x–y diagram for a feed that enters as saturated vapour?
questions.why: For saturated vapour q = 0, so the slope q/(q − 1) is zero and the line is horizontal at y = z. A vertical line corresponds to q = 1, a saturated liquid feed. The q-line lies along the diagonal only in the limit of infinitely large |q|, not for a vapour feed. A slope of −1 corresponds to q = 0.5, a feed that is half vapour.

questions.q: A column separates 100 kmol/h of a saturated-liquid feed with 40 mol% of the light component into a distillate of 95 mol% and bottoms of 5 mol%, with a total condenser and R = 2. Find D, B, the flows in each section and the equations of both operating lines, and show they meet on the q-line.
markScheme: q = 1 so L′ = L + F = 177.8 and V′ = V = 116.7 kmol/h (1 mark)
Both give y = 0.583 at x = 0.40, on the vertical q-line (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: D = 100(0.40 − 0.05)/(0.95 − 0.05) = 38.9 kmol/h; B = 61.1 kmol/h. L = 2 × 38.9 = 77.8 and V = 3 × 38.9 = 116.7 kmol/h. Saturated liquid feed (q = 1): L′ = 77.8 + 100 = 177.8 kmol/h, V′ = 116.7 kmol/h. Rectifying: y = (2/3)x + 0.95/3 = 0.667x + 0.317. Stripping: y = (177.8/116.7)x − 61.1 × 0.05/116.7 = 1.524x − 0.0262. At x = 0.40: rectifying gives 0.583 and stripping gives 0.6095 − 0.0262 = 0.583, so they meet on the vertical q-line at x = z.

questions.q: A binary separation with constant α = 2 must give x_D = 0.90 and x_B = 0.10. What is the minimum number of equilibrium stages from the Fenske equation?
questions.why: N_min = ln[(0.9/0.1)(0.9/0.1)]/ln 2 = ln 81/ln 2 = 4.394/0.693 = 6.3. 3.2 uses only the distillate ratio, ln 9/ln 2, leaving out the bottoms term. 40.5 divides 81 by α instead of dividing the logarithms. 0.16 inverts the formula, ln 2/ln 81.

questions.q: What happens as the reflux ratio is reduced towards its minimum value at fixed product specifications?
options: The number of stages needed rises towards infinity
The number of stages falls to its minimum
The operating lines move onto the 45° line
questions.why: Lower reflux moves the operating lines towards the equilibrium curve; at R_min they touch it and the steps never pass the pinch, so infinitely many stages are needed. The minimum number of stages occurs at total reflux, the opposite limit. Reboiler duty falls with less reflux, because less vapour is generated. Operating lines lie on the 45° line only at total reflux.

questions.q: For a binary separation with α = 2.5, x_D = 0.95, x_B = 0.05 and a saturated liquid feed with z = 0.40, calculate N_min and R_min. If the column has 12 theoretical trays plus a partial reboiler, how many actual trays are needed for an overall efficiency of 70%?
markScheme: Round up to 18 trays, reboiler counted separately (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Fenske: N_min = ln[(0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05)]/ln 2.5 = ln 361/0.916 = 5.889/0.916 = 6.4 stages (including the reboiler). For q = 1 the pinch is at x′ = 0.40, y′ = 2.5 × 0.4/(1 + 1.5 × 0.4) = 0.625. R_min/(R_min + 1) = (0.95 − 0.625)/(0.95 − 0.40) = 0.591, so R_min = 0.591/0.409 = 1.44. The reboiler is treated as an equilibrium stage on its own, so the 12 theoretical trays need 12/0.70 = 17.1, rounded up to 18 actual trays.

questions.q: A dilute solute is absorbed from a gas into pure solvent with equilibrium y = 2x. 95% of the solute must be recovered. What is the minimum liquid-to-gas ratio (L/G)_min?
questions.why: With x_in = 0 and x_out* = y_in/m, (L/G)_min = (0.95y_in)/(y_in/2) = 2 × 0.95 = 1.9. 2.0 would correspond to complete (100%) recovery. 2.1 divides m by the recovery instead of multiplying. 0.1 multiplies m by the fraction not recovered (0.05) rather than the fraction recovered.

questions.q: An absorber operates with absorption factor A = L/(mG) = 0.8. Which statement is true?
options: Even with infinitely many stages, the fraction of solute absorbed cannot exceed about 80%
Any recovery can be reached if enough stages are added
The column is at minimum reflux
The operating line lies below the equilibrium line, so the column strips instead
questions.why: With A < 1 the operating line is less steep than the equilibrium line and meets it at the gas inlet end, so the solvent saturates; for pure solvent the limiting recovery equals A, here 80%. Unlimited recovery requires A > 1. Minimum reflux is a distillation concept; the analogue here is minimum L/G, which applies to a particular recovery, not to A = 0.8 itself. The operating line still lies above the equilibrium line (in the limit it only touches it at the gas-inlet end), so the column does absorb; the recovery is just limited.

questions.q: A gas containing 2 mol% of a solute is scrubbed in a counter-current tray column with solute-free solvent to recover 90% of the solute. The dilute equilibrium line is y = 1.5x. The liquid rate is 1.5 times the minimum. Find (L/G)_min, the actual L/G, the outlet liquid composition, and the number of equilibrium stages using the Kremser equation.
markScheme: Kremser expression evaluated: ln[10(1 − 0.741) + 0.741] = ln 3.33 (1 mark)

questions.q: For a dilute system with k_y = 0.05 kmol/m² s, k_x = 0.5 kmol/m² s and equilibrium y = 2x, what is the overall gas-phase coefficient K_y?
questions.why: 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x = 20 + 2/0.5 = 24, so K_y = 0.0417 kmol/m² s. 0.55 adds the film coefficients instead of their resistances. 0.0455 leaves out m in the liquid-film term (1/K_y = 20 + 2 = 22). 0.05 assumes the gas film is the only resistance, ignoring the 17% contributed by the liquid film.

questions.q: Absorption of which gas into water is most likely to be gas-film controlled?
questions.why: Ammonia is extremely soluble in water, so m is small and the liquid-film term m/k_x is negligible, leaving the gas film in control. Oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen are all sparingly soluble, giving large m, so the liquid-film resistance dominates.

questions.q: A packed absorber treats a dilute gas from y_in = 0.020 to y_out = 0.002 using solute-free solvent at L/G = 2.025, with equilibrium y = 1.5x. H_OG is 0.5 m. Using the log-mean driving force, find N_OG and the packed height.

A solute is extracted from a carrier with an immiscible solvent in a single equilibrium stage. The distribution coefficient (mass-ratio basis) is 3 and equal masses of solvent and carrier are used. What fraction of the solute is extracted?
questions.why: E = K_D S/F = 3, so the fraction left in the raffinate is 1/(1 + E) = 0.25 and the fraction extracted is 0.75. 0.25 is the fraction left behind, not extracted. 0.67 is 1 − 1/E, which wrongly takes 1/E as the fraction remaining. 0.50 assumes the solute splits equally because equal masses of liquid are used, ignoring the distribution coefficient.

questions.q: For the same total solvent and the same number of stages, which arrangement leaves the least solute in the final raffinate?
options: Crosscurrent cascade with fresh solvent split equally between stages
A single stage using all the solvent
All three give the same result
questions.why: In counter-current flow the most depleted raffinate meets the freshest solvent, so a driving force is maintained along the cascade. Crosscurrent is better than one stage but wastes solvent capacity, because each portion leaves only partly loaded. A single stage is limited to one equilibrium contact. They are not the same: with E = 2 and two stages, the fractions left are 14%, 25% and 33% respectively.

questions.q: 100 kg of an aqueous carrier containing a solute is treated with 50 kg of an immiscible solvent. The distribution coefficient on a mass-ratio basis is K_D = 4. Find the fraction of solute left in the raffinate for (a) one stage, (b) two crosscurrent stages with 25 kg of solvent each, and (c) two counter-current stages with all 50 kg.
markScheme: Comment that counter-current uses the solvent most effectively (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: E = 4 × 50/100 = 2. (a) Single stage: fraction left = 1/(1 + E) = 1/3 = 0.333. (b) Each crosscurrent stage uses 25 kg, so E = 1 per stage and each stage leaves half: (1/2)² = 0.25. (c) Counter-current with N = 2: (E − 1)/(E^(N+1) − 1) = (2 − 1)/(8 − 1) = 0.143. Counter-current makes the best use of the same solvent because the leanest raffinate always meets the freshest solvent.

questions.q: In a sieve-tray column, liquid is observed draining through the perforations rather than flowing across the tray. What is this called, and what causes it?
options: Weeping, caused by too low a vapour rate
Flooding, caused by too high a vapour rate
Entrainment, caused by too high a vapour rate
questions.why: When the vapour rate is too low, the pressure under the tray cannot hold the liquid up, so it weeps through the holes. Flooding occurs at high flow rates, when liquid backs up and fills the column. Entrainment carries liquid upwards as droplets, the opposite direction to weeping. Foaming produces a stable froth that can cause premature flooding, but it is not the downward drainage described.

questions.q: A column must handle 2 m³/s of vapour. The flooding velocity is 1.30 m/s and the design is at 80% of flooding. Ignoring downcomer area, what diameter is needed?
questions.why: Design velocity = 0.8 × 1.30 = 1.04 m/s, area = 2/1.04 = 1.92 m², and D = √(4 × 1.92/π) = 1.56 m. 1.40 m is the diameter at 100% of flooding, leaving no margin. 1.92 is the area in m², not a diameter. 2.44 m is 4A/π without taking the square root.

questions.q: Explain the main operating limits of a tray column and how they define its operating window, and give two situations in which a packed column would usually be preferred.
markScheme: Flooding at high vapour/liquid rates (downcomer backup or excessive entrainment) sets the upper limit (1 mark)
Entrainment at high vapour velocity reduces efficiency (1 mark)
Weeping/dumping at low vapour rate sets the lower limit; the window lies between (1 mark)
Two valid packed-column cases, e.g. small diameter, vacuum/low pressure drop, corrosive or foaming systems (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: At high vapour and liquid loads a tray column floods: liquid backs up in the downcomers or is carried upward until the column fills, so separation collapses. Before that, high vapour velocities cause entrainment of droplets to the tray above, which lowers tray efficiency. At low vapour rates the vapour cannot support the liquid on the tray, so it weeps (or, worse, dumps) through the holes. Satisfactory operation lies in the window between weeping and flooding/excess entrainment. Packed columns are generally preferred for small-diameter columns, for vacuum service where low pressure drop matters, and for corrosive or foaming systems.

questions.q:
A continuous distillation column with a total condenser and partial reboiler separates 100 kmol/h of a saturated liquid feed containing 40 mol% of the more volatile component A. The distillate must contain 95 mol% A and the bottoms 5 mol% A. The relative volatility is constant at 2.5 and constant molal overflow may be assumed.
(a) Calculate the distillate and bottoms flows. [3]
(b) Find the minimum reflux ratio and the minimum number of equilibrium stages. [6]
(c) For R = 2.0, write the equations of both operating lines. [5]
(d) Determine the number of equilibrium stages and the optimal feed stage, explaining your method. [7]
(e) If the overall tray efficiency is 70%, how many actual trays are needed? Comment on the choice of R. [4]
markScheme: D = 38.9, B = 61.1 kmol/h from overall and component balances (3 marks)
Pinch at q-line/equilibrium intersection: y′ = 0.625; R_min = 1.44 (3 marks)
Rectifying y = 0.667x + 0.317; L′ = 177.8, V′ = 116.7; stripping y = 1.524x − 0.0262 (5 marks)
Method: step from (0.95, 0.95) between equilibrium curve and operating lines, switching at the intersection (2 marks)
Result: 13 equilibrium stages including the reboiler, feed on stage 7 from the top (5 marks)
12 theoretical trays/0.7 = 17.1 so 18 actual trays plus reboiler (2 marks)
Comment: R/R_min = 1.38 lies within the usual range; trade-off between stages and energy (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) F = D + B; 0.40 × 100 = 0.95D + 0.05B. Hence D = 100(0.40 − 0.05)/(0.95 − 0.05) = 38.9 kmol/h and B = 61.1 kmol/h.

(b) Saturated liquid feed: q = 1, so the q-line is vertical at x = 0.40. Equilibrium there: y′ = 2.5 × 0.4/(1 + 1.5 × 0.4) = 0.625. With the pinch at (0.40, 0.625):
R_min/(R_min + 1) = (0.95 − 0.625)/(0.95 − 0.40) = 0.591, so R_min = 1.44. (The equilibrium curve has constant α and no inflexion, so the pinch is at the feed.)
Fenske: N_min = ln[(0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05)]/ln 2.5 = ln 361/ln 2.5 = 5.889/0.916 = 6.4 equilibrium stages, including the reboiler.

(c) L = RD = 77.8 kmol/h; V = (R + 1)D = 116.7 kmol/h.
Rectifying: y = (R/(R + 1))x + x_D/(R + 1) = 0.667x + 0.317.
q = 1: L′ = L + F = 177.8 kmol/h; V′ = V = 116.7 kmol/h.
Stripping: y = (L′/V′)x − Bx_B/V′ = 1.524x − 0.0262.
Both lines give y = 0.583 at x = 0.40, confirming they meet on the q-line.

(d) Starting at (x_D, x_D) = (0.95, 0.95), alternate between equilibrium, x = y/(α − (α − 1)y), and the operating line. Stage-by-stage (y leaving, x leaving):
1: 0.950, 0.884; 2: 0.906, 0.794; 3: 0.846, 0.687; 4: 0.775, 0.579; 5: 0.703, 0.486; 6: 0.641, 0.416; 7: 0.594, 0.369.
Stage 7 is the first whose liquid falls below x = 0.40, so it straddles the intersection: it is the optimal feed stage and the stripping line is used from here on.
8: 0.537, 0.317; 9: 0.456, 0.251; 10: 0.357, 0.181; 11: 0.250, 0.118; 12: 0.153, 0.068; 13: 0.077, 0.032.
x = 0.032 is below x_B = 0.05, so 13 equilibrium stages are needed (12 trays plus the partial reboiler, with a slight over-separation on the last stage), with the feed on stage 7 from the top. This matches a graphical McCabe–Thiele construction.

(e) The reboiler is one equilibrium stage, leaving 12 theoretical trays: 12/0.70 = 17.1, so 18 actual trays plus the reboiler.
R = 2.0 is 1.38 R_min, inside the usual range of roughly 1.2–1.5 R_min. The column needs about twice N_min. A lower R would cut reboiler and condenser duties (V = (R + 1)D) but add stages quickly as R approaches R_min; a higher R would save trays but cost more energy and a wider column.

questions.q:
A gas stream containing 2 mol% of a soluble pollutant is to be treated by counter-current absorption into a solute-free solvent so that 90% of the pollutant is removed. The system is dilute and the equilibrium line is y = 1.5x. The solvent rate is set at 1.5 times the minimum.
(a) Find (L/G)_min, the actual L/G and the outlet liquid composition. [5]
(b) Find the number of equilibrium stages for a tray column. [5]
(c) For a packed column with H_OG = 0.5 m, find N_OG and the packed height, and the corresponding HETP. [6]
(d) Explain how raising the operating pressure would affect the design. [4]
markScheme: N_OG ≈ 4.64 via log-mean or closed form (3 marks)
Z = 2.3 m; HETP = Z/N ≈ 0.58 m, consistent with H_OG ln(1/A)/(1/A − 1) (3 marks)
Higher pressure: m = H/P falls, so solubility rises, (L/G)_min falls; at fixed L/G, A rises and fewer stages/smaller height are needed (3 marks)
Trade-off: compression cost and pressure-rated equipment (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) y_out = (1 − 0.9) × 0.02 = 0.002. At minimum solvent the outlet liquid is in equilibrium with the inlet gas: x_out* = 0.02/1.5 = 0.0133. (L/G)_min = (0.02 − 0.002)/(0.0133 − 0) = 1.35. Actual L/G = 1.5 × 1.35 = 2.025. Balance: x_out = 0.018/2.025 = 0.0089.

(b) A = (L/G)/m = 2.025/1.5 = 1.35, 1/A = 0.741. With x_in = 0, Kremser gives
N = ln[(y_in/y_out)(1 − 1/A) + 1/A]/ln A = ln[10 × 0.259 + 0.741]/ln 1.35 = ln 3.333/0.300 = 1.204/0.300 = 4.0 equilibrium stages.

(c) Driving forces: bottom y − y* = 0.02 − 1.5 × 0.0089 = 0.00667; top 0.002 − 0 = 0.002. Δy_lm = (0.00667 − 0.002)/ln(3.333) = 0.00388. N_OG = 0.018/0.00388 = 4.64. (Check: closed form [1/(1 − 0.741)] × ln 3.333 = 3.857 × 1.204 = 4.64.)
Z = H_OG × N_OG = 0.5 × 4.64 = 2.3 m. HETP = Z/N = 2.32/4.01 = 0.58 m, the same as H_OG ln(1/A)/(1/A − 1) = 0.5 × 0.300/0.259 = 0.58 m. N_OG exceeds N because A > 1.

(d) For an ideal gas phase m = H/P, so raising the pressure lowers m and makes the solute more soluble. (L/G)_min = m × recovery falls in proportion, so less solvent is needed for the same recovery. At a fixed L/G, A = L/(mG) rises, the operating and equilibrium lines move further apart, and both N and N_OG fall, giving a shorter column. Higher gas density also reduces the gas volumetric flow, so the column diameter can be smaller. Against this, compressing the gas costs energy and the column must be pressure-rated, so the optimum balances these costs; for regenerable solvents, stripping is then done at low pressure.
